questions.q: Per this lesson, what should be confirmed first when an incident is reported?
options: That the problem is actually real and matches what's being reported
The exact root cause, before anything else
Who is ultimately responsible for the failure
Whether a backup exists
questions.explain: Chasing a phantom or misreported problem wastes the most valuable early minutes of an incident.

questions.q: After confirming a problem is real, what does this lesson say to assess next?
options: Blast radius and severity — how much is affected and how urgent it is
The exact line of code or query that caused it
Whether the DBA on call should be replaced
The full historical audit log for the affected table
questions.explain: Severity and blast radius determine urgency and who needs to know, before root cause is investigated.

questions.q: What does 'stabilize before you root-cause' mean in this lesson's framework?
options: Making the immediate symptom stop (e.g., killing a runaway query) before fully understanding why it happened
Skipping root-cause analysis entirely, forever
Restoring from backup as the very first action
Waiting for the problem to resolve itself before doing anything
questions.explain: The priority in the first phase of an incident is stopping the bleeding, not fully explaining it — root-causing happens after things are stable.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should communication about incident status happen?
options: Throughout the incident, in parallel with the technical response — not only after it's resolved
Only after the root cause has been fully identified
Only if a customer specifically asks for an update
Never — communication should wait until a formal postmortem
questions.explain: Silence during an active incident is its own failure; status communication runs the whole time, independent of technical progress.

questions.q: What is the risk of treating every incident as maximum severity, per this lesson?
options: It burns trust and energy over time by over-escalating issues that don't warrant it
It guarantees faster root-cause identification
It has no real downside
It automatically triggers a full database restore
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns that over-treating minor incidents as maximum severity has a real cost, just as under-treating a real outage does.
